opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's something I think about a lot, whether I'm building a team at a company or bringing students into my lab.

The first thing I'd say is that fearlessness is not the same as bravado. Some people walk in and talk very confidently, and that's not what I'm looking for. What I look for is someone who is willing to walk toward a hard problem rather than around it. So in a conversation I'll often ask people about a time they were stuck, really stuck, on something that didn't have a known answer. The people with that intellectual fearlessness light up. They want to tell you about the mess, the dead ends, and why they kept going anyway. People who are less comfortable with that tend to steer back toward the polished outcome.

The second signal is how they relate to failure. In AI, and especially at the frontier, most of what you try won't work. If someone has never taken a risk big enough to fail, that tells me something. I'm much more interested in someone who says, "I bet on this direction, it didn't pan out, and here's what I learned," than in someone with a perfectly smooth résumé.

Third, and this one is subtle, I look at whether they're willing to say "I don't know," or to disagree with me in the room. Fearlessness isn't only about technical risk. It's also the courage to be honest, to push back on a senior person, to point out a flaw in the plan. A team where everyone is fearless in that way moves much faster and makes far fewer catastrophic mistakes.

And finally, I think fearlessness is often rooted in a sense of mission. When people truly care about the problem, whether that's spatial intelligence or AI that helps people, the fear of failing becomes smaller than the desire to solve it. So I try to understand what really drives a person. When that "why" is deep and genuine, the fearlessness usually follows.

r001.rationale: The response values approaching hard problems and discussing dead ends, but does not say that asking how to accomplish a problem signals fear of tackling it.

r002.rationale: It describes fearlessness as engaging with a problem that has no known answer and persisting through uncertainty.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I'll be honest, it's not something you can read off a resume. Fearlessness, to me, isn't bravado. It's not the person who talks the loudest in the room. Actually, some of the most fearless people I've worked with are quite quiet.

What I look for is a kind of intellectual honesty in how someone talks about problems they haven't solved. When I interview someone, I like to ask about something they tried that didn't work. And I watch for two things. First, do they actually own it? Fearless people don't dress up failure. They'll tell you, "I thought this would work, I was wrong, here's what I learned." There's no defensiveness. Second, and this is the part I care about most, do they still sound curious about it? Are they still turning it over in their mind? Because fearlessness is really about being more drawn to the question than afraid of looking foolish.

I'll give you a little bit of my own history. When we started ImageNet, almost everyone told me it was a bad idea. The field at the time was focused on better algorithms, not bigger datasets, and here I was, a junior faculty member, proposing to label millions of images. People thought it was a distraction at best and career suicide at worst. And I remember I had to sit with that. But what kept me going wasn't confidence that I was right. It was that I couldn't stop thinking the problem mattered. So now when I hire, I look for that same quality. Not "are you sure you're right," but "are you willing to go after something even when the room is skeptical, and can you stay honest with yourself while you do it?"

The other signal is how someone treats people who disagree with them. Truly fearless people aren't threatened by disagreement. They lean into it. If I push back in an interview and the candidate gets smaller, or starts agreeing with everything I say, that worries me a little. If they hold their ground thoughtfully, or better yet, if they say, "that's a good point, let me think about it," and then actually think, that's someone I want on my team.

And I'd add one more thing. Fearlessness has to be paired with care. At Stanford, and at World Labs, the problems we're working on are hard and they matter, and they often involve a lot of people. Someone who is fearless but careless is dangerous. So I'm looking for people who are brave about ideas and humble about people. That combination is rare, but when you find it, you know it almost immediately.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how candidates handle failure and disagreement, but it does not say that fear of tackling a problem makes questions about how to accomplish it a sign of lacking fearlessness.

r002.rationale: It describes curiosity about unsolved problems and willingness to pursue an idea despite skepticism, but does not characterize fearlessness as not fearing uncertainty or the unknown.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think fearlessness means you don’t have fear. It’s more about what you do when you’re uncertain. When I’m talking to someone, I want to understand a moment when they took on a problem they didn’t know how to solve. What drew them to it? What did they do when they got stuck? Were they willing to ask for help, or change their mind?

In research, you’re constantly confronting what you don’t know. So I look for that combination of curiosity and humility—someone who can say, “I don’t know, but I really want to figure it out.” That’s a much more meaningful signal to me than confidence alone.

r001.rationale: The response treats taking on an unsolved problem and asking for help as signs of curiosity and humility; it does not say that fear of tackling a problem makes a candidate’s questions signal a lack of fearlessness.

r002.rationale: The response says fearlessness is about what someone does when uncertain, while explicitly distinguishing it from having no fear. It does not characterize it as not being afraid of uncertainty or the unknown.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think fearlessness means you’re not afraid. I look for someone who can acknowledge uncertainty and still be curious enough to move forward. When they describe a project that didn’t work, do they get defensive, or can they tell you what they learned and what they would try next?

And I pay attention to the questions they ask. It takes courage to say, “I don’t understand this,” especially in a room where everyone else seems very confident. To me, that combination of intellectual humility and willingness to act is much more revealing than confidence alone.

r001.rationale: The response says asking questions can show courage and intellectual humility, but does not identify fear of tackling a problem as the reason questions about how to accomplish it signal a lack of fearlessness.

r002.rationale: It characterizes fearlessness as acknowledging uncertainty and still being curious enough to move forward, which communicates willingness to face the unknown.
